title: Architecture in One Level
objective: After this level you can explain what architects do and how buildings changed over time.
summary: Vitruvius: good building needs firmness, commodity and delight. Architects design and draw what builders build, and building moved from mud brick and stone to iron, glass and steel.

cards.headline: The oldest surviving book on architecture says a building needs three things.
cards.body: The Roman architect Vitruvius wrote it about 2,000 years ago, and it's the only complete book on architecture to survive from ancient Greece and Rome. Architects still quote his list. Here it is, plus what architects actually do and how building changed.

mascot.line: Firmness first. Delight is lovely, but it's hard to admire a ceiling that's on the floor.

cards.headline: Firmness, commodity, delight
cards.body: Vitruvius named three principles: firmitas, utilitas and venustas. A famous 1624 English version made them firmness, commodity and delight. Firmness means strength: it stands up. Commodity means it's useful to the people inside. Delight means it's beautiful. Miss one and the building fails: a gorgeous house with a leaky roof, or a sturdy box nobody can bear to look at. This chapter is all about the first one.

cards.headline: The chief builder
cards.body: Architect comes from the Greek arkhitekton: arkhi-, chief, plus tekton, builder. Today an architect helps a client pin down what they need, designs the building, and produces drawings with technical specifications that builders can price and build from. They advise on approvals like planning permission, and they can inspect the work on site. An architect rarely lays a brick. The drawings say where every one goes.

title: Why Buildings Stand Up
objective: After this level you can explain how weight flows down through a building to the ground.
summary: Buildings carry dead loads (themselves) and live loads (people, weather). Every load follows a load path to the soil, and each part is squeezed (compression) or stretched (tension).

cards.headline: Every building is carrying something heavy: itself.
cards.body: Before anyone walks in, a building is already holding up its own floors, walls and roof. Standing up means getting all of that weight, plus yours, safely down into the ground. Here's how.

cards.headline: Dead loads and live loads
cards.body: Engineers sort weight into two kinds. Dead loads are permanent: the structure's own weight plus its roofing, flooring, pipes and inside walls. Live loads come and go: people, sofas, pianos, books, cars. Weather counts as a live load too, and wind pushes sideways rather than down. A floor has to be ready for both, including the day your friend moves in with a piano.

mascot.line: Next time you stand on a floor, you are part of a load path. Welcome aboard.

cards.headline: Follow the weight down
cards.body: Every load needs a route to the ground, and engineers call that route the load path. A continuous path runs from the roof, through the walls, to the foundation, and finally into the soil that holds the building up. Here's an analogy: a stack of books on a table. The bottom book carries every book above it, and the table carries the lot. Take one link out and the weight has nowhere to go.

cards.fact: Every piece of that path is being squeezed or stretched.
cards.context: Engineers name two basic forces. Compression pushes and squeezes; tension pulls and stretches. A post carrying weight down to the ground is squeezed. A cable holding up a hanging load is stretched. Keep both words handy: the rest of this chapter is about which parts get squeezed, which get stretched, and which materials can take it.

title: Posts and Beams
objective: After this level you can explain the post-and-lintel system.
summary: Two posts and a lintel: Stonehenge and every doorway. A loaded beam is squeezed on top and stretched below, and stone is weak when stretched, so stone lintels stay short.

cards.headline: Stonehenge's builders used carpentry joints on solid stone.
cards.body: Its lintels sit on the uprights with mortise-and-tenon joints and lock to each other with tongue-and-groove joints, the kind usually found only in woodworking. Under all that joinery is the oldest trick in building: two posts and a beam across the top.

cards.headline: Posts and a lintel
cards.body: Architects call it the post-and-lintel system: two upright posts hold up a horizontal lintel laid across their tops. Stonehenge is built this way, and the system was the basis of architecture from prehistoric to Roman times. It never really left. Look at the top of the nearest door or window: the beam across that opening is still called a lintel.

cards.headline: The beam's problem: it bends
cards.body: Load a beam and it sags a little. Its top is squeezed in compression while its underside is stretched in tension: Level 2's two forces, in one piece. Stone and brick are brittle and weak in tension, so a long stone beam is in trouble along its underside. That's why stone and brick can only make short lintels.
cards.callout: Try it: bend a ruler. The top face squeezes and the bottom face stretches.

mascot.line: Stone is a champion at being squeezed. Ask it to stretch and it simply refuses.

cards.fact: Short beams mean crowded posts.
cards.context: If every stone lintel has to stay short, the posts holding them must stand close together. A wide room on stone posts and beams needs a lot of posts in the way. To open up bigger spaces, builders needed a new shape, one that never asked stone to stretch. That's the next level.

title: The Arch
objective: After this level you can explain how an arch carries weight.
summary: Wedge-shaped voussoirs locked by a keystone turn weight into compression. Arches push outward (thrust), so supports must be massive, and they span far wider than stone lintels.

cards.headline: An arch can't stand up until its very last stone goes in.
cards.body: Until then, builders prop it up on a temporary wooden frame called centering. Set the top stone, take the frame away, and the whole curve holds itself up. What changed?

cards.headline: Wedges that squeeze together
cards.body: An arch is built from wedge-shaped blocks called voussoirs, each cut to press firmly against its neighbors. The central one, set last, is the keystone. Weight pressing down forces the wedges together instead of apart, so the whole curve stays in compression. Remember Level 3's problem: stone is weak when stretched. An arch never asks it to stretch.

mascot.line: Every arch is quietly shoving its neighbors. Good supports just shove back.

cards.headline: The push at the feet
cards.body: The catch: an arch doesn't only push down. It also pushes outward at its feet, a diagonal force called thrust. Left unchecked, thrust makes the arch collapse, so its supports must be massive enough to resist it and carry it down into the foundation. Here's an analogy: lean two playing cards together on a slippery table. Their bottoms slide apart unless something blocks them.

cards.fact: Small blocks, wide openings.
cards.context: A stone lintel has to be one massive piece, and Level 3 showed it can only be short. An arch can span much wider openings, because it's made of small blocks of brick or stone that are easy to carry. The Romans put the semicircular arch to work in bridges, aqueducts and large buildings.

title: Domes
objective: After this level you can explain how a dome spreads its weight.
summary: A dome evolved from the arch and pushes out all around its rim. Its hoop forces stretch toward the base, so Florence's record masonry dome (1436) wears tie rings like barrel hoops.

cards.headline: A dome can do something an arch can't: stand while it's half built.
cards.body: Level 4's arch needed a wooden frame until its keystone went in. A dome can rise ring by ring with no frame at all. The secret is in its circles.

cards.headline: An arch, spun around
cards.body: A dome is a rounded roof that evolved from the arch. Here's an analogy: picture an arch spun all the way around its middle. An arch pushes outward at its two feet; a dome pushes outward all around its rim. That's why early giant domes, like Rome's Pantheon, sat on heavy supporting walls.

cards.headline: Rings that squeeze, rings that stretch
cards.body: A dome has a trick an arch lacks. Besides the forces running down its curve, it carries hoop forces around it, in horizontal rings. Near the top the rings squeeze, so each finished ring holds itself in place. Lower down, the rings are stretched instead, and masonry hates stretching. So masonry domes tend to crack along lines running from top to rim, splitting into slices (think orange segments) whose bases lean outward.

mascot.line: The strongest part of that dome is the part nobody gets to see. Classic.

cards.fact: Florence's dome wears hidden hoops.
cards.context: Florence Cathedral's dome, completed in 1436, is still the largest masonry dome in the world. Filippo Brunelleschi built it without formwork, and he bound it with tie rings: stone beams held by metal cramps, and oak timbers joined by metal connectors. As an analogy, think of the hoops on a barrel, holding in the lower part that wants to spread.

title: Stone, Brick and Wood
objective: After this level you can compare the oldest building materials.
summary: Stone: strong squeezed, weak stretched, fireproof. Brick: sun-dried mud, then kiln-fired. Wood: strong for its weight but burns, so London rebuilt in brick after 1666.

cards.headline: In 1666, London burned. It came back as a city of brick.
cards.body: After the Great Fire, London changed from a city of wood into a city of brick, for one reason: protection from fire. Every building material is a trade-off like that. Here are the three oldest.

cards.headline: Where wood beat stone
cards.body: Remember Level 3's short stone lintels? Wood did better. Greek builders swapped stone beams for wooden ones, because wood needed fewer supports, which opened up the space inside. Wood is also strong for its weight and easy to work. Its great weakness is the one London learned about in 1666.

mascot.line: Mud, sun, then fire. Honestly, bricks have had quite a glow-up.

cards.fact: Baking a brick changes it.
cards.context: The first bricks were mud, shaped and dried in the sun. Fire them in a kiln and they gain strength, hardness and resistance to heat. At Ur, in Mesopotamia, potters discovered the closed kiln, in which the heat could be controlled. And ancient brickmakers kept each brick small enough for one person to handle easily: small, easy-to-carry blocks, just what Level 4's arches need.

title: Concrete
objective: After this level you can explain Roman and modern concrete.
summary: Roman concrete of lime, ash and rock holds up the largest unreinforced concrete dome. A 2023 study suggests it self-heals. Modern concrete uses portland cement and steel bars.

cards.headline: The world's largest unreinforced concrete dome is almost 1,900 years old.
cards.body: It tops Rome's Pantheon, rebuilt under the emperor Hadrian between 118 and 128 CE, with no steel inside at all. So what did the Romans know? And why do builders today hide steel inside theirs?

cards.headline: The Roman recipe
cards.body: Roman concrete mixed lime with volcanic ash and chunks of volcanic rock. Level 1's Vitruvius recorded that the best concrete for building in the sea used ash from around the Gulf of Naples. It worked: Roman harbor structures have survived 2,000 years underwater. Your garden path should be so lucky.

mascot.line: Notice the word 'may' up there. Good science keeps its claims the right size.

cards.fact: Roman concrete may patch its own cracks.
cards.context: That's the finding of a 2023 MIT-led study of concrete from the Roman site of Privernum. Its little white lumps, called lime clasts, were long blamed on sloppy mixing. The study says they formed when builders mixed in hot quicklime. When a crack reaches a clast and water gets in, dissolved calcium refills the crack as calcium carbonate. Test samples made this way sealed their cracks within two weeks. These are one study's findings, not a verdict on every Roman building.

cards.headline: Modern concrete, and a gardener's tubs
cards.body: Modern concrete is bound with portland cement, which Joseph Aspdin made in 1824 by burning and grinding limestone and clay. But concrete shares Level 3's stone problem: strong when squeezed, weak when stretched. The fix is usually credited to Joseph Monier, a Paris gardener who reinforced his concrete tubs with iron mesh and patented the idea in 1867. In reinforced concrete, steel bars take the tension and the concrete takes the compression.

title: Steel and Glass
objective: After this level you can explain how steel frames and glass walls changed building.
summary: In a frame building a skeleton carries the floors, so walls can be glass. The Crystal Palace (1851) rose within six months; steel, strong when stretched, suits frames.

cards.headline: In 1851, a gardener designed a building with walls of glass.
cards.body: Joseph Paxton ran the gardens at Chatsworth and built glasshouses there. For the Great Exhibition in London's Hyde Park, he designed the Crystal Palace: slender iron holding up walls of clear glass. How can a wall be made of glass?

cards.headline: Walls that carry, or a frame that carries
cards.body: Until now in this chapter, walls and posts did the carrying: each wall held up the floors above it, on Level 2's load path. A frame building splits the jobs. A skeleton of columns and beams carries the floors, and the outer wall only has to hold up itself. Here's an analogy: your bones hold you up, and your skin just wraps you. Once a wall carries nothing but itself, it can be thin, even glass.

mascot.line: Doodling in meetings: usually frowned upon. Occasionally world-famous.

cards.fact: The Crystal Palace went up within six months.
cards.context: Paxton drew his first sketch on blotting paper during a railway board meeting, following the lines of the lily house he'd built at Chatsworth. The building was made of prefabricated parts of iron and sheet glass, made in advance and put together on site. A giant building, fast: the frame idea and the factory idea arrived together.

cards.headline: Why steel suits the frame
cards.body: Stone and cast iron share a weakness: both are weak when stretched. Steel isn't. It has high tensile strength, which suits Level 3's beams, stretched along their undersides. In 1884–85, Chicago's Home Insurance Building rose on an iron and steel skeleton; it's generally considered the first tall building held up that way. Later chapters take that skeleton all the way to the sky.

title: Blueprints
objective: After this level you can explain how plans and drawings guide builders.
summary: Plans are horizontal cuts, sections vertical cuts, elevations faces, all drawn to scale. Herschel's 1842 cyanotype made blueprints: white lines on blue.

cards.headline: Blueprints were blue because of sunlight and iron.
cards.body: For decades, builders worked from copies with white lines on a deep blue background. The color was pure chemistry, and you'll see how. But first: what's actually drawn on them?

cards.headline: Three ways to slice a building
cards.body: Architects show a building in standard views. A plan is a horizontal cut, usually taken about three to four feet above the floor, seen from above. A section is a vertical cut, showing how the floors stack up. An elevation shows one vertical face straight on, like the front of a house. Here's an analogy: slice a layer cake across for a plan, cut it down the middle for a section, and look at its side for an elevation.

cards.headline: Drawn to scale
cards.body: Every line is drawn to scale. At one half inch to one foot, each half inch on paper stands for a whole foot of building, so a builder can measure a wall that doesn't exist yet. That's the handover Level 1's architect makes: drawings with technical specifications to build from. Even Level 8's blotting-paper doodle was turned into proper drawings within a week.

mascot.line: A building plan printed by the Sun. Architecture has always had friends in high places.

cards.fact: The first blueprints were sun prints.
cards.context: John Herschel introduced the cyanotype in 1842: paper treated with two iron compounds turns blue where light hits it. Lay a drawing on see-through material over the paper, expose it to light, and the lines come out white on dark blue. It caught on for copying drawings in the 1870s. By the 1950s, diazo prints had replaced it in most offices, but the word lives on: since 1926 it has also meant any detailed plan.

title: Checkpoint: How Buildings Stand
objective: After this level you can explain how walls, arches and domes carry weight.
summary: A hanging chain in tension, flipped, is an arch in compression (Hooke, 1675). Engineers check masonry by finding a line of thrust inside it.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 finale: hang a chain, flip it over, and you've drawn an arch.
cards.body: In 1675, the scientist Robert Hooke hid that idea in a Latin anagram. It ties this whole chapter together: squeeze and stretch, arches and domes, and the stone that holds them up.

cards.headline: As hangs the chain
cards.body: Unscrambled, Hooke's anagram said: "As hangs the flexible line, so but inverted will stand the rigid arch." A hanging chain is in tension, with every force running along its curve. Flip the shape and those forces become compression, still running along the curve, so the arch doesn't bend or buckle. Level 2's two forces turn out to be mirror images.

mascot.line: Squeeze inside the stone: safe. Squeeze poking out: time to call an engineer.

cards.headline: Keep the squeeze inside the stone
cards.body: Engineers check old arches and domes with the same idea. They treat masonry as having no strength in tension (Level 3's stone lintels agree). Then they look for a line of thrust, the path the squeezing force takes, lying entirely inside the masonry. If one fits, the structure can be shown to be safe for those loads. Level 5's cracked domes show what happens where masonry is asked to stretch.

title: The First Buildings
objective: After this level you can describe the earliest houses and temples.
summary: Göbekli Tepe's pillar enclosures rose about 11,500 years ago, built by hunter-gatherers, and people lived there too. Çatalhöyük packed mud-brick houses with no streets.

cards.headline: Which came first, the house or the temple?
cards.body: You'd bet on the house: settle down first, then build something grand for the gods. One of the oldest monumental sites ever found makes that bet look shaky. Here are the first buildings, and the arguments about them.

cards.headline: A monument before farms
cards.body: Göbekli Tepe, in southeastern Turkey, was built by hunter-gatherers, before farming, beginning about 11,500 years ago. They raised T-shaped limestone pillars over 5 meters tall, some weighing up to 50 tons, in great round and oval enclosures. Its first excavator, Klaus Schmidt, read it as a ritual center: a place people gathered, but didn't live. A temple, in other words, with no town attached.

mascot.line: Archaeologists changing their minds when new evidence turns up: that's the system working.

cards.headline: Then the hearths turned up
cards.body: Digs in recent years found hearths, domestic buildings and a big rainwater cistern cut into the bedrock. People seem to have lived at Göbekli Tepe after all, right beside the great enclosures. So the temple label is now argued over, and the honest answer to the hook may be: both at once. One trench can rewrite a textbook.

cards.headline: A town with no streets
cards.body: At Çatalhöyük, also in Turkey, people lived from about 6700 BCE in rectangular mud-brick houses packed wall to wall, with no streets in between. The rooftops were the streets. You walked across your neighbors' roofs, then climbed down a wooden ladder through an opening in your own ceiling. Old houses were filled in and rebuilt on top, over and over, until the town became a hill.

cards.fact: Some of the oldest furniture on Earth is stone.
cards.context: At Skara Brae in Orkney, Scotland, a storm in 1850 uncovered a village about 5,000 years old, the best-preserved Neolithic settlement in Western Europe. Its houses still hold their stone dressers and box beds, right where their owners left them. Built-in furniture, long before flat-pack.

title: Ziggurats
objective: After this level you can explain Mesopotamian ziggurats.
summary: A ziggurat was a solid stepped tower of mud brick in a waterproof skin of baked brick and bitumen, with weeper holes. At Aqar Quf, reed layers reinforce the core.

cards.headline: A ziggurat is a giant tower you can't go inside.
cards.body: Staircases climbed its sides to a temple on the top. Inside there was nothing at all: no rooms, no corridors, just brick. So how do you keep a solid mountain of mud brick standing?

cards.headline: A mountain with no rooms
cards.body: A ziggurat was a stepped temple tower of ancient Mesopotamia, usually square or rectangular, with no internal chambers. About 25 are known. The best known, at Ur, dates to about 2100 BCE, under King Ur-Nammu. Three staircases led up to a temple on its flat top. All that brick was, in effect, one enormous pedestal.
cards.callout: Legend check: the Tower of Babel is popularly linked to Babylon's ziggurat. Linked, not proven.

cards.headline: A raincoat with vents
cards.body: Every ziggurat had a core of mud brick and a skin of baked brick. At Ur, the core took several million sun-dried bricks. The facing bricks were mortared with bitumen, a natural tar, to make a waterproof surface: Level 6's kiln-fired brick, hard and strong, doing the weather work. The skin was also pierced by weeper holes that let water evaporate from the core. A raincoat, with vents.

mascot.line: Reeds: cheap, local, and still holding a tower together. Not bad for a plant.

cards.fact: Some ziggurats were reinforced with reeds.
cards.context: At Aqar Quf in Iraq, after every eight or nine courses of bricks, the builders laid a layer of reed matting bedded in sand and gravel. Plaited reed ropes run right through the tower from side to side as reinforcement, and the matting kept the structure from slumping sideways when it got wet. Here's an analogy: Level 7's steel bars do a similar job inside concrete today.

title: The Pyramids of Giza
objective: After this level you can explain how the pyramids were engineered.
summary: The Great Pyramid used limestone for bulk and granite for the King's Chamber. Five compartments above its flat ceiling, topped by a gabled roof, help carry the weight.

cards.headline: Deep inside the Great Pyramid, a flat stone ceiling holds up a mountain.
cards.body: The pyramid is some 2.3 million blocks, about 5.75 million tons of stone, finished about 4,500 years ago. A flat stone ceiling is Level 3's lintel, and Level 3 showed how badly stone takes stretching. So how has that ceiling held?

cards.headline: The right stone for each job
cards.body: The Great Pyramid's builders chose stone by job. The core is yellowish limestone blocks. The outer casing and the inner passages used finer, light-colored limestone. And the burial chamber, the King's Chamber, is built of huge granite blocks: lined with granite, and roofed with it. Plain stone for the bulk, fine stone for the finish, granite for the room that mattered most.

cards.headline: Five rooms stacked on a ceiling
cards.body: Directly above the King's Chamber sit five low compartments, stacked one on another and separated by massive horizontal granite slabs. They were probably built to shield the chamber's ceiling, diverting the immense thrust of the masonry above. Here's an analogy: a stack of trays held over a cake, so the weight lands on the trays first.

mascot.line: Five spare rooms nobody was ever meant to visit. Some of the hardest-working rooms in history.

cards.fact: The top compartment has a pointed roof.
cards.context: The highest of the five compartments has a gabled roof: huge limestone blocks set in leaning pairs, like the two sides of a house roof, helping to bear the weight above. Remember Level 3: a flat stone beam is stretched along its underside. Leaning blocks press against each other instead, a bit like Level 4's arch wedges. A flat ceiling, a stack of slabs, and a point on top.

title: Egyptian Temples
objective: After this level you can describe Karnak and its forest of columns.
summary: Karnak's Great Hypostyle Hall: 134 columns under stone lintels, a tall lit central aisle. Egyptian temples ran from gateway to a dark, raised sanctuary.

cards.headline: Almost all of Notre-Dame cathedral could fit inside one hall at Karnak.
cards.body: Karnak's Great Hypostyle Hall covers nearly an acre. Walk in, though, and it won't feel like a big open space. It feels like a forest. Why fill a room with columns?

cards.headline: Under pillars
cards.body: Hypostyle means 'under pillars': a room whose roof rests on columns. The interiors of Egyptian temples were lined with columns covered by stone lintels. And Level 3 showed why stone lintels stay short: stone is weak when stretched. Short beams mean crowded posts. At Karnak, that means 134 columns under one roof.

cards.headline: A tall aisle with windows
cards.body: The columns aren't all alike. Down the middle stand 12 giants about 20 m tall, topped with open papyrus flowers. The other 122, about 14 m tall, end in closed buds. The height difference left room for clerestory windows: huge stone grilles high up beside the central aisle. They were the hall's only daylight. With its stone roof on, it stood in twilight even at midday.

mascot.line: A building that gets quieter and darker the closer you get to its heart. Very dramatic. Very on purpose.

cards.headline: A walk back to the beginning of the world
cards.body: An Egyptian temple ran in a line: a pylon gateway, an open court, the hypostyle hall, then the sanctuary with the god's statue. The court may have been as far as anyone but priests could go. The papyrus columns recalled the marshes around the mound of creation. The sanctuary was the darkest, most enclosed room, with the highest floor: the mound itself. Every step in was darker, higher and more exclusive.

summary: The Seven Wonders: two tombs, two statues, a temple, gardens and a lighthouse. Fire, earthquakes and stone recycling took six; the oldest, the pyramids, survives.

cards.headline: Ancient travelers had a must-see list. Six of its seven sights are gone.
cards.body: One of the best-known versions was written by the Greek writer Antipater of Sidon in the 2nd century BCE. Here's the list, how six of its wonders fell, and which one is still standing.

cards.headline: Fire, earthquakes and borrowed stone
cards.body: The Temple of Artemis was burned in 356 BCE by a man named Herostratus, rebuilt, and later wrecked by invading Goths. The Colossus of Rhodes, shaped bronze plates fastened to an iron framework, was toppled by an earthquake about 226 BCE, little more than half a century after it was finished. The Mausoleum probably fell to an earthquake centuries later, and its stones went into local buildings. Flames, tremors, and neighbors who needed good stone.

cards.fact: The Hanging Gardens may never have hung in Babylon.
cards.context: Tradition says King Nebuchadnezzar II built them for his wife, Amytis, who missed the green mountains of her homeland. It's a lovely legend, but no certain trace of the gardens has been found at Babylon. One modern theory puts them at Nineveh instead, built by King Sennacherib. The list's great mystery is a wonder that might not have been where everyone said.

mascot.line: Level 13 showed you the inside of the survivor. Solid stone ages well.

cards.fact: The last wonder standing is the oldest.
cards.context: The Pyramids of Giza are the oldest of the seven and the only one still substantially in existence. The Mausoleum did leave us a word, though. Artemisia built it for her husband, Mausolus, and every grand tomb since has been a mausoleum.

title: The Parthenon
objective: After this level you can explain the Parthenon's hidden curves.
summary: The Parthenon's base curves, its columns swell and lean inward. Built without mortar, its blocks were hand-fitted and joined with lead-sealed iron clamps.

cards.headline: The Parthenon has few truly straight lines. It still took precision to build.
cards.body: Athena's temple in Athens was designed by Ictinus and Callicrates and built from 447 BCE in about eight or nine years. Outside, it's a ring of columns carrying stone lintels. Look closer and almost nothing is quite straight.

cards.headline: Nothing quite straight
cards.body: The Parthenon's base curves gently upward toward the middle. Its columns taper, but also swell slightly partway up, a bulge called entasis. They aren't vertical either: they slope imperceptibly inward. And the corner columns are a little thicker than the rest. The classic explanation is that each tweak corrects a trick of the eye, such as a row of straight columns looking thin in the middle. That explanation is still debated.

cards.headline: No mortar, no gaps
cards.body: The Parthenon was built without mortar, so there was nothing to fill a bad fit: every block had to be trimmed by hand. The joints are all but invisible, even under a magnifying glass. Neighboring blocks were locked together with iron clamps set in carved grooves, and the builders poured molten lead over them, sealing the iron away.

mascot.line: Skipping one step of an ancient recipe. We've all done it with flat-pack furniture.

cards.fact: In 1898, a restoration began cracking the marble.
cards.context: From 1898, the architect Nikolaos Balanos restored the Parthenon with iron clamps, but left off the lead coating. Rain swelled the bare iron, and the swelling cracked the marble. Today's restorers are replacing his clamps with titanium, which won't corrode. The ancient builders had the better trick all along: wrap the iron.

title: The Colosseum
objective: After this level you can explain how the Colosseum handled about 50,000 people.
summary: The Colosseum: a freestanding oval of travertine, tufa and concrete vaults ringed by arcades. 76 numbered entrances, class zones and vomitoria moved its crowds.

cards.headline: Up to 50,000 people, one building, and every ticket numbered.
cards.body: Getting that many people in, seated and out again is a design problem. The Colosseum solved it with a ring of arches and a lot of numbers.

cards.headline: A mountain made of arches
cards.body: The Colosseum is a freestanding oval about 189 by 156 m. A framework of travertine stone carries it, with walls of volcanic tufa and concrete, and inside runs a honeycomb of barrel and groin vaults. Outside, three stories of arcades wrap all the way around, framed by engaged columns in the Doric, Ionic and Corinthian orders. It's Level 4's Roman arch, repeated around and around.

cards.headline: Find your number
cards.body: The Colosseum had at least 80 entrances at ground level. Seventy-six were numbered, and tickets were sold for each, so your ticket told you which arch to walk through. Inside, the seats were split into zones by class, with wooden seats and standing room at the very top for women and the poor. Your gate, your zone, your seat: a plan any stadium today would recognize.

mascot.line: Tell someone this at the next big game. They'll never look at the exit signs the same way.

cards.fact: A vomitorium is for crowds, not for being sick.
cards.context: A vomitorium is an entrance passage that pierces the banks of seats in a theater, amphitheater or stadium. The name comes from the Latin vomere, 'to vomit', because the passages disgorged the spectators. So the word describes crowds leaving, not dinner coming back.

title: Aqueducts
objective: After this level you can explain how aqueducts carried water downhill over long distances.
summary: Aqueducts ran on gravity, so the slope had to hold: Nîmes's fell only 25 to 34 cm per km. Surveyors leveled with a chorobates; arches crossed valleys.

cards.headline: One Roman aqueduct fell only about 25 to 34 cm every kilometer.
cards.body: It carried water about 50 km to Nîmes, in southern France, and surveys differ on the exact slope. Either way, it's gentle: less than the height of a bowling pin per kilometer. Gravity did all the work, so that slope had to hold across hills and valleys. How do you build that?

cards.headline: Downhill, mostly underground
cards.body: Roman aqueducts moved water by gravity alone, so the channel had to keep its slope wherever the land went. Mostly, that meant underground. Of the roughly 420 km of aqueducts serving Rome, only about 50 km crossed valleys on stone arches; the rest ran in conduits below ground. The famous arches are the rare places where the valley dropped away and the water couldn't.

mascot.line: A plumb line and a bit of water. Sometimes the best tools are the ones with nothing to break.

cards.headline: A spirit level as long as a room
cards.body: To hold a slope, you first need to know what level is. Level 1's Vitruvius described the tool: the chorobates, a straightedge about twenty feet long on two legs, with plumb lines hanging beside marked lines. When the plumb lines matched their marks, it stood level. On a windy day you could pour water into a groove along its top and read the level off the water instead.

cards.fact: The Pont du Gard stands without mortar.
cards.context: Where the Nîmes aqueduct crossed the Gard River, the Romans built the Pont du Gard: three tiers of arches, with the water channel along the top. It was built without mortar. Level 4 explains how that works: weight presses each arch's wedge-shaped stones together, keeping the whole curve in compression.

title: The Pantheon
objective: After this level you can explain how the Pantheon's dome has stood for 1,900 years.
summary: The Pantheon's concrete grades from basalt to pumice on 6 m walls. Its lower dome cracked top to rim, as Level 5 predicts, and now stands as a ring of arches.

cards.headline: The Pantheon's dome is cracked. It has stood for almost 1,900 years anyway.
cards.body: Level 7 named it the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome, about 43 m across. Level 5 predicted where masonry domes crack. So why is this one still up?

cards.headline: Heavy at the bottom, light at the top
cards.body: The Romans graded their materials by height: heavy basalt in the foundations, brick and tufa higher up, and the lightest stone, pumice, toward the center of the vault. Level 5 said big domes push outward all around their rim, so they need heavy walls. The Pantheon's are 6 m thick, strengthened by brick arches built one above another inside them. Pack it like a suitcase: heavy things at the bottom.

cards.headline: Cracks, right where Level 5 said
cards.body: Remember Level 5: in a masonry dome, the hoop forces stretch toward the base, and domes tend to crack into slices. The Pantheon did exactly that. Its cracks run top to rim through the lower half of the dome, and they stop short of the oculus, the round opening at the top. The engineers Robert Mark and Paul Hutchinson analyzed the result in 1986.

mascot.line: A dome that turned its cracks into arches. Honestly, that is a very Roman way to deal with a problem.

cards.fact: A cracked dome becomes a ring of arches.

title: Hagia Sophia
objective: After this level you can explain Hagia Sophia's floating dome.
summary: Pendentives turn Hagia Sophia's square into a circle for its dome; 40 windows make it float and half domes brace it. The first dome partly fell in 558, and the new one was raised to push out less.

cards.headline: Hagia Sophia's first dome fell in. The one that replaced it still stands.
cards.body: Justinian's great church in Constantinople went up between 532 and 537, under a dome so wide and bright it seemed to float. Twenty-one years later, part of it came down. How do you set a giant dome on a square church, and how do you keep it up there?

mascot.line: Square room, round dome. Good thing the job went to a mathematician and a physicist.

cards.headline: A circle on a square
cards.body: A dome needs a round rim to sit on, but Hagia Sophia was planned around a square. Its designers, Anthemius of Tralles, an architect and mathematician, and Isidorus of Miletus, a professor of physics, used pendentives: curved triangles of masonry filling each upper corner, so that the tops join into a circle. Two pairs of great arches meet on the pendentives, which carry the dome's load down four massive piers. Picture a round lid on a square box, with the corners filled in to catch it.

cards.headline: Forty windows and two half domes
cards.body: Forty windows ring the base of the dome, so daylight breaks up the solid stone beneath it and the dome seems almost suspended. That's the delight. The firmness hides east and west, where two giant half domes join the arches and stretch the covered space lengthwise. Engineers treat a half dome like this as a buttress. Remember Level 5's dome, pushing outward all around its rim? The half domes help take that push.

cards.fact: The second dome was built taller on purpose.
cards.context: After an earthquake, part of the first dome collapsed in 558. An account in ASCE's Civil Engineering magazine blames its shallow shape, which put its load on the walls instead of cleanly down the piers. Isidorus the Younger rebuilt it by 562, raising its crown by about 6 meters to reduce the sideways thrust, and adding 40 ribs. A steeper dome pushes out less.

title: Great Mosques
objective: After this level you can describe great mosques from Córdoba to Istanbul.
summary: A mosque is built around the qibla, the direction of Mecca, marked by the mihrab. Córdoba's hall of columns grew by moving its qibla wall; Sinan based Istanbul's Süleymaniye on Hagia Sophia.

cards.headline: A mosque is designed around a direction.
cards.body: Before anyone chooses columns or domes, a mosque has to know one thing: which way Mecca lies. Everything else can change, and at Córdoba and Istanbul, it did.

cards.headline: The wall that points to Mecca
cards.body: Muslims face Mecca to pray, and a mosque is built to match. That direction is the qibla, and the wall facing it holds the mihrab, a niche for the imam who leads the prayer. Beside it stands the minbar, a pulpit of steps for the preacher. Outside rises the minaret, the tower from which the muezzin gives the call to prayer five times each day. Think of a mosque as a building with a compass built in.

cards.headline: Córdoba: a forest you can extend
cards.body: The Umayyad ruler Abd al-Rahman I built the Great Mosque of Córdoba, in Spain, in 784–786: a prayer hall roofed on rows of columns carrying arches. That plan grows easily. When the city's population grew, Abd al-Rahman II extended the hall southward, knocking down the old qibla wall and building a new one farther out. Extensions in the 9th and 10th centuries doubled the mosque's size, and today some 850 pillars hold up its roof. Need more room? Add more rows.

mascot.line: Good architects borrow. Great ones borrow, then build the thing a little better organized.

cards.fact: Istanbul's grandest mosque took its cue from a church.
cards.context: Sinan was chief architect of the Ottoman Empire for about the last 40 years of his life. His Süleymaniye Mosque, built for Sultan Süleyman in 1550–1557, was based on the design of Level 21's Hagia Sophia. Sinan made the huge central dome the focal point around which the rest of the building was planned, with smaller domes and buttresses leading up to it. Same big idea, a new faith's building.

title: Round Arches and Thick Walls
objective: After this level you can describe Romanesque churches.
summary: Barrel vaults are rows of arches pushing out all along, so walls were thick. Groin vaults gather the push at four corners; Durham (1093) added stone ribs.

cards.headline: Put a stone ceiling on a church, and the walls have to wrestle it.
cards.body: Romanesque builders roofed their churches with stone vaults. Level 4 already warned what arches do: they push outward. So how do you hold a stone ceiling up without it shoving the walls apart?

cards.headline: A tunnel made of arches
cards.body: Romanesque churches used round arches for windows, doors and arcades, and many roofed the nave with a barrel vault: in effect a continuous row of arches, deep enough to cover a room, like half a tunnel. Every one of those arches pushes out, so a barrel vault must be held in along its entire length by heavy walls with few openings. That's why these churches have massive piers and walls with few windows. Big holes would weaken the very walls doing the holding.

cards.headline: Cross two tunnels
cards.body: Cross two barrel vaults at right angles and you get a groin vault. Repeated in a row, groin vaults can cover a long rectangular space. The trick is where the push goes: it gathers at the four corners, so only those points need buttressing, and the wall between them no longer has to be massive. Here's an analogy: a table carries its top on four legs, not on solid sides.

mascot.line: Look up in an old church. If you see stone ribs crossing the ceiling, you're looking at its skeleton.

cards.fact: Durham Cathedral's ceiling hides a stone skeleton.
cards.context: Durham Cathedral in England, begun in 1093, is an outstanding Romanesque church. Its builders set stone ribs, forming pointed arches, to support the vault: the earliest known example. The ribs carry the vault at critical points, so the stone filling between them could be thinner and lighter. The vault has stood for 900 years. Next level, Gothic builders take that skeleton and run.

title: Gothic Cathedrals
objective: After this level you can explain flying buttresses and pointed arches.
summary: Pointed arches of different spans rise to one height; flying buttresses carry the vault's thrust across the aisle to outer piers, steadied by pinnacles.

cards.headline: Gothic builders took the heavy supports and moved them outdoors.
cards.body: Level 23's churches held their vaults in with thick walls. At the abbey church of Saint-Denis near Paris, rebuilt about 1135 to 1144, builders combined the rib vault, the pointed arch and the flying buttress into one system. Here's how the pieces work.

cards.headline: The adjustable arch
cards.body: A round arch is stuck with rigid geometry: its height is set by its width. That's awkward when vault ribs cross a rectangular bay, because the short sides, long sides and diagonals all want different heights. A pointed arch escapes the trap. Sharpen or relax the point, and arches of different spans rise to the same height, meeting neatly at the top. With pointed arches and rib vaults like Durham's, Gothic builders could cover far more complicated plans. Think of it as an arch that comes in adjustable sizes.

cards.headline: A half arch in the air
cards.body: Gothic vaults still pushed outward, just as Level 4's thrust says they must, and the supports still had to be massive enough to resist it. The answer was the flying buttress: a half arch that springs from the upper part of the wall and carries the vault's thrust across the aisle to an outer pier. Level 4's massive supports are all still there. They've simply moved outdoors, clear of the wall.

mascot.line: Next time you see a cathedral bristling with little spires, you'll know: those are paperweights.

cards.fact: The little spires on top are there for their weight.
cards.context: A pier holding a flying buttress is often crowned with a pinnacle. It adds weight, and weight makes the pier more stable against the push arriving from the vault. The flying buttress itself evolved from simpler supports hidden from view, and its extra supporting power is what made the high ceilings of Gothic churches possible. Decoration, yes, but decoration with a job.

title: Walls of Light
objective: After this level you can explain how Gothic builders filled churches with light.
summary: A Gothic cathedral is a stone skeleton, so walls became windows: Chartres's tall clerestory, thin bar tracery, and iron hidden in the stone from the 1160s.

cards.headline: A Gothic cathedral is Level 8's glass building, done in stone.
cards.body: Once ribs and buttresses carried the vault, the wall between them had far less to do. Gothic builders turned it into windows. Three things made that work: a skeleton, stone lace and some hidden iron.

cards.headline: A skeleton with windows
cards.body: Level 8's frame building splits the jobs: a skeleton carries the floors, and the outer wall only holds itself. A Gothic cathedral works the same way in stone. Ribs, piers and flying buttresses do the carrying, so the wall between them can open into larger windows. At Chartres, mainly built after 1194, the architect dropped the gallery level and used specially designed flying buttresses to enlarge the clerestory, the windowed wall rising above the aisle roofs. After Chartres, great churches were meant to be dominated by glass set high up.

cards.headline: Stone lace
cards.body: Even a window needs stone to hold its glass. Early Gothic windows used plate tracery: openings cut through a solid slab of stone, as at Chartres in the 12th century. Then came bar tracery, developed after 1220, with early examples at Reims Cathedral: thin upright stone bars dividing the glass. Thinner stone, more glass. The window stopped being a hole in a wall and started being the wall.

mascot.line: Stone gets the credit, glass gets the photos, and the iron quietly holds everything together.

cards.fact: Notre-Dame was held together with iron from the start.
cards.context: The 2019 fire let researchers sample Notre-Dame de Paris's iron staples, and a 2023 study dated those in its galleries to about the 1160s, the first phase of building. That makes Notre-Dame the first known Gothic cathedral to use iron massively as a real building material. By the mid-13th century, builders were embedding iron chain links at the tops of walls, as at the Sainte-Chapelle. Walls of glass, it turns out, had iron in their bones.

title: Angkor Wat
objective: After this level you can describe the temple city of Angkor.
summary: Angkor Wat (12th century, for Vishnu) models the Hindu cosmos: towers for Mount Meru, a moat for the oceans, in a Khmer capital built around water.

cards.headline: The temple on Cambodia's flag is a model of the universe.
cards.body: Angkor Wat appears on the Cambodian flag, and Britannica calls it the world's largest religious structure, covering some 400 acres. Its builders weren't just making a big temple. They were building a map of the cosmos you could walk into.

mascot.line: Most buildings have a floor plan. This one has a cosmology.

cards.headline: A mountain in stone
cards.body: The Khmer king Suryavarman II built Angkor Wat in the 12th century and dedicated it to the Hindu god Vishnu. Its five central towers stand for the peaks of Mount Meru, the sacred mountain of Hindu cosmology. Its enormous moat, about 200 meters wide, suggests the oceans at the edge of the world. So when you walk in over the moat, you've symbolically crossed the ocean to reach the mountain of the gods.

cards.headline: A temple in a city of water
cards.body: Angkor was the capital of the Khmer Empire from the 9th to the 15th century. One of its most notable features was a vast system of reservoirs, canals and moats. They watered the fields, and they also stood for the cosmic waters. So Angkor Wat's moat wasn't a one-off. The temple was one piece of a whole city built around water, practical and symbolic at once.

cards.fact: The stone may have arrived by canal.
cards.context: Angkor Wat is built on laterite encased in sandstone quarried in the Kulen Hills. In 2012, Etsuo Uchida and Ichita Shimoda of Waseda University used satellite images to trace canals from more than 50 quarries at the foot of Mount Kulen to Angkor: a route less than half as long as the overland one once assumed. If you're moving a mountain's worth of stone, float it.

title: Pagodas
objective: After this level you can explain how tall wooden pagodas survive earthquakes.
summary: Pagodas grew from the stupa. At Hōryū-ji each story is its own frame, the joints can slide, and the central pillar carries only the spire.

cards.headline: Tall, thin and wooden sounds like the wrong recipe for earthquake country.
cards.body: Yet engineers studying Japan's Hōryū-ji pagoda found no historical record of a five-story pagoda toppling in an earthquake. After the 1995 Kobe earthquake, no serious damage to old wooden pagodas nearby was reported. What do they know that a stiff tower doesn't?

cards.headline: A tower built for relics
cards.body: A pagoda is a Buddhist tower that grew out of the stupa, a domed monument first built in ancient India to house relics. Five-story pagodas were built to enshrine remains of the Buddha. The form reached Japan from India by way of China, with Buddhism, in the 6th century. The pagoda at Hōryū-ji, in Nara, was rebuilt around 711 after a fire, and it's regarded as Japan's oldest wooden pagoda.

mascot.line: Sometimes the strongest move is not to hold on too tightly. Pagodas figured that out a long time ago.

cards.headline: Five stories that don't hold hands
cards.body: In the Hōryū-ji pagoda, no column ties the stories together: each is its own framework, set on the one below. Even the ground-floor columns aren't fixed to the foundation. Researchers credit the pagoda's survival to friction and sliding in its many wooden joints, and to its deep eaves, which work like a balancing toy. A stiff tower fights a quake. A pagoda shimmies.

cards.fact: The central pillar holds up almost nothing.
cards.context: Down the middle runs the shinbashira, the central column. At Hōryū-ji it supports only the ornamental spire on top, independently of the main structure. So what is it for? One explanation: when a quake makes the heavy roofs try to slide sideways, the pole won't let any of them move very far. It's less a backbone than a bouncer.

cards.headline: The womb house

It's the innermost and most sacred sanctuary, housing the main image or emblem of the temple's deity, and it's small. Over it rises the temple's tower: in northern India a shikhara, in the south a pyramidal vimana. The holiest room sits at the foot of the tallest peak, like a cave under a mountain.

mascot.line: Two temples, thousands of kilometers apart, both reaching for the same mountain.

Its steeply rising towers and mountain-like form refer to Mount Meru, the mythical source of creation. Many miniature shrines climb its spire, pulling your eye upward peak by peak. Sound familiar? title: Castles
objective: After this level you can explain how castles were designed for defense.
summary: Castles were lords' homes built to be attacked. Mining under a wall brought Rochester's corner down in 1215, so towers turned round, and projecting towers and machicolations covered the wall's foot.

cards.headline: In 1215, a king brought down a castle tower with the fat of 40 pigs.
cards.body: A castle was generally the home of a king or lord, built as a stronghold, ready to be attacked. Rochester Castle's keep is the tallest such building to survive in Europe, and King John wanted it. So in 1215 his men went underneath it.

cards.headline: Dig, prop, burn
cards.body: The most powerful way to attack a castle wall was mining. Attackers dug a tunnel beneath it and held up the roof with wooden props. Then they set the props on fire, and the masonry above collapsed. At Rochester, the miners went for the keep's south-east corner turret, and the burning pig fat fired their props. Down came the corner. Remember Level 2's load path? A mine takes away the bottom of it.

mascot.line: No corners, no easy place to start digging. Sometimes the best defense is geometry.

cards.headline: Lose the corners
cards.body: Square towers had a weak spot: their corners. Miners could tunnel under a corner, fill the hole with wood and light it, and the tower would partly collapse. So builders changed the shape. Towers projecting from castle walls were square at first but later round, and many rectangular keeps were replaced with circular ones. Rochester tells the story in stone: the square turret John's miners destroyed was rebuilt semicircular.

cards.fact: Castle towers stick out from the wall on purpose.
cards.context: From a tower that protrudes, defenders can shoot along the wall's face and foot, where attackers try to dig. Towers also rose higher than the wall, for extra range. Later came machicolations: permanent stone galleries overhanging the wall top, with openings to drop missiles on anyone directly below. Each of these shapes answers an attack.

title: The Great Wall
objective: After this level you can explain how the Great Wall of China was built over centuries.
summary: Not one wall: Qin joined older walls around 220 BCE; the Ming built the best-preserved one. Rammed earth to granite, it blends into the land, so it is hard to see from orbit.

cards.headline: You can't see the Great Wall from the Moon. And it isn't one wall.
cards.body: It was built by a series of governments over about 2,000 years, not as one long, unbroken stretch. NASA says it isn't visible from the Moon at all. So how do you build a wall across centuries, and why is it so hard to spot?

cards.headline: Joined up, then rebuilt
cards.body: Border walls were already standing when Qin Shi Huang, first emperor of a unified China, had them joined into one around 220 BCE. Most of that wall was rammed earth and wood. Much later, the Ming dynasty (1368-1644) built the most extensive and best-preserved version, adding watchtowers and platforms. Most familiar photos of the wall show Ming work. Add up every section ever built and you get about 21,196 km.

cards.headline: Built from what was there
cards.body: There's no single Great Wall recipe. Some sections are rammed earth: soil packed hard. Others are brick, and elsewhere builders used quarried granite or even marble blocks. The Ming improved their mortar too. Researchers at Zhejiang University found sticky rice mixed into its lime. Level 7's Romans mixed lime with volcanic ash; the Ming reached for the rice pot.

mascot.line: Thousands of kilometres long, and still camouflaged. That takes talent.

cards.fact: The Great Wall hides in its own landscape.
cards.context: The wall looks a lot like the stone and soil around it, so it's hard to make out with the human eye even from low Earth orbit. NASA puts it plainly: it isn't visible from the Moon, and it's difficult or impossible to see from Earth orbit without high-powered lenses.

cards.headline: Home, office and throne room
cards.body: Augustus had his house on the Palatine. Later, Nero built a splendid residence on the same hill, and the hill's name stuck to the buildings. Today a palace is a royal residence that is sometimes also a seat of government or a religious centre. So a palace is where a ruler sleeps, and often also where the ruling gets done. Think of it as a home with the office downstairs.

mascot.line: Castle: keep them out. Palace: let them in, and make sure they are impressed.

title: The Forbidden City
objective: After this level you can describe Beijing's palace city.
summary: Begun 1406, occupied 1420, barred to most subjects. Buildings are ranked on a south-facing axis, and the halls are timber post-and-lintel frames. A museum since 1925.

cards.headline: For five centuries, most people were barred from China's palace.
cards.body: That's the Forbidden City's name explained: access was barred to most of the realm's subjects. The Yongle emperor of the Ming dynasty commissioned it in 1406, and the court moved in in 1420. So what was behind the wall?

mascot.line: Face south, line up, know your rank. Even the buildings had manners.

cards.headline: A city where everything lines up
cards.body: Just what Level 33 described: not one building but many, behind a high wall and a moat about 52 metres wide. Inside, the most important buildings stand on a north-south axis and face south, to honour the Sun. The Palace Museum says every structure followed the traditional architectural hierarchy, designed to reflect imperial power. Here, where a building stood told you how much it mattered.

cards.headline: Up the terraces to the throne
cards.body: In the Outer Court, three main halls of government stand on a three-tiered marble terrace above an immense plaza. The grandest is the Hall of Supreme Harmony, home of the emperor's throne and the largest single building in the compound. Behind the Outer Court, the Inner Court held the imperial living quarters. Government at the front, family at the back.

cards.context: Its halls are timber buildings with post-and-lintel frames under tiled roofs: posts holding up beams, like Stonehenge. title: The Alhambra
objective: After this level you can describe the Alhambra's courtyards and carvings.
summary: Behind plain rammed-earth fortress walls, the Nasrids' Alhambra turns inward: rooms around courtyards like the Court of the Myrtles, water brought from the Darro, and walls of tile and carved stucco.

cards.headline: From outside, the Alhambra looks like a fortress. Step inside.
cards.body: Its highly ornate rooms and patios contrast with the plain walls of the fortress outside. Built on a plateau above Granada, chiefly between 1238 and 1358 by the Nasrid dynasty, its name means 'the red' in Arabic, probably after the reddish rammed earth of those outer walls.

cards.headline: Rooms around a pool
cards.body: A dark, winding passage leads you into the Court of the Myrtles. At its centre lies a large reflecting pool set in marble paving, and the palace around it appears again in the still water. Rooms open onto the courtyard, and the palace comes with its own mirror.

mascot.line: Fountains indoors. Medieval air conditioning, with a soundtrack.

cards.headline: Water on a hilltop
cards.body: The Royal Canal took water from the Darro river 11 km upstream, and it made the hill habitable. The Nasrids then brought the sound, sight and coolness of water everywhere: into gardens, courtyards, marble canals and even indoors. Plumbing, raised to poetry.

cards.fact: Above eye level, the Alhambra's walls are carved plaster.
cards.context: Geometric tiles cover the lower walls. Above them, carved stucco (plaster) runs in bands and panels of curving patterns and calligraphy. The stucco of the Comares facade was once painted in brilliant colours; only traces remain. The plain fortress outside was just the wrapping paper.

title: The Taj Mahal
objective: After this level you can explain how and why the Taj Mahal was built.
summary: Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal as a tomb for Mumtaz Mahal, from about 1632. Symmetry, outward-leaning minarets and pietra dura are design; the cut-off hands are legend.

cards.headline: The Taj Mahal is a tomb.
cards.body: The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan built it for his wife, Mumtaz Mahal, who died in childbirth in 1631. Both their cenotaphs now stand in its central chamber. How was it built, and which famous stories about it are true?

cards.headline: A 22-year building site
cards.body: Building began about 1632, and the tomb itself was finished by about 1638-39. The whole complex took 22 years. More than 20,000 workers came from India, Persia, the Ottoman Empire and Europe. The chief architect was probably Ustad Ahmad Lahawri. Note the 'probably': even the architect's name comes with a question mark.

mascot.line: Even the towers were designed to fall politely.

cards.headline: Balance on every side
cards.body: The tomb has four nearly identical facades, a central dome about 73 metres high ringed by four smaller domes, and a minaret at each corner. On one side stands a red sandstone mosque; on the other stands its identical twin, the jawab, which balances it. And the minarets lean slightly outward, so in a disaster such as an earthquake they would fall away from the tomb, not onto it.

cards.fact: The Taj Mahal's flowers are made of stone.
cards.context: Its white marble is decorated with pietra dura, Italian for 'hard stone': semiprecious stones such as lapis lazuli, jade and turquoise, inlaid in geometric and floral designs. Nobody painted these petals. Each one is cut stone, set into cut stone.

cards.headline: Two legends, labeled
cards.body: Legend: Shah Jahan had the builders' hands cut off. Historians have found no evidence for it. Legend: he planned a black marble twin across the river. Some historians dismiss that too. The documented story, a grieving emperor and 20,000 workers, is remarkable enough.

title: Versailles
objective: After this level you can describe Versailles and its Hall of Mirrors.
summary: Louis XIV turned a hunting lodge into an immense palace that from 1682 held the whole court, keeping nobles under his eye. Its Hall of Mirrors (1678-84) boasted 357 mirrors when mirrors were a luxury.

cards.headline: Versailles started as a hunting lodge.
cards.body: It was built for Louis XIII in the 1620s. His son Louis XIV transformed it, between 1661 and 1710, into an immense palace. Why would a king need that much house?

mascot.line: A palace big enough for every rival. Very generous. Very watchful.

cards.headline: Room for everyone who mattered
cards.body: From 1682 Versailles was the official royal residence, with room to house the whole court. That was the point. Under the king's watchful eye, the nobility could no longer plot against the throne; the great lords were kept eager to serve and please him. The best way to watch your rivals is to invite them to move in.

cards.headline: The Hall of Mirrors
cards.body: Jules Hardouin-Mansart built it from 1678 to 1684, replacing an open terrace onto the garden. The gallery runs more than 70 metres, with 17 arches of mirrors facing 17 windows: 357 mirrors in all. Overhead, Charles Le Brun's 30 ceiling paintings tell the story of Louis XIV's reign. Guess who's the hero.

cards.fact: A wall of mirrors was a wall of money.
cards.context: At the time, mirrors were a great luxury, and Venice held a monopoly on making them. This hall showed that France's new mirror manufacture could rival Venice. Courtiers crossed it daily, so every walk to work was a small advertisement.

title: Machu Picchu
objective: After this level you can explain how the Inca built with stone and no mortar.
summary: Machu Picchu's main walls are blocks fitted almost perfectly and held by gravity, not mortar. They can move in place in quakes, and half or more of the effort is underground.

cards.headline: At Machu Picchu, when an earthquake hits, only the restorations fall.
cards.body: That's how Yale archaeologist Richard Burger puts it. The Inca estate, probably built in the mid-15th century for the ruler Pachacuti, stands on main walls held together by gravity, not mortar. How does that work?

cards.headline: Held together by gravity
cards.body: The builders joined massive stone blocks almost perfectly, beside and on top of each other, with nothing in between. Some blocks are polygonal, each shaped exactly for its place in the wall; one famous stone in Cusco has 12 sides. The Inca knew about mortar. A few small structures on the site use it. They just left it out of the biggest walls.

mascot.line: A great story with a footnote. The footnote is part of the lesson.

cards.headline: Walls that can shrug
cards.body: Those walls are thousands of interlocking, irregular blocks, and it's suggested that this makes them tougher in earthquakes: the stones can move in place. In a massive earthquake in 1650, many Spanish colonial buildings in Cusco collapsed, while the Inca walls there and at Machu Picchu were unharmed. One honest caveat from historian Stella Nair: the evidence is anecdotal, without actual seismic research.

cards.fact: Most of the work is buried.
cards.context: Engineer Kenneth Wright estimates the Inca spent about 50 to 60 percent of their building effort underground, on foundations and site preparation. Under the main plaza, his team found topsoil over sandy gravel over a drainage layer of granite chips left from stone cutting. With about 76 inches of rain a year, Wright says, without good drainage there would be no Machu Picchu.

title: Fairy-Tale Castles

summary: Neuschwanstein (begun 1869 for Ludwig II) copies no real castle: stage-set designs mixing old motifs. Behind the knightly look: brick, steel, central heating, telephones.

cards.headline: The world's most famous 'medieval' castle had telephones.
cards.body: Neuschwanstein, in Bavaria, was begun in 1869 for King Ludwig II, who built it to withdraw from public life. It was still unfinished when he died in 1886, and within weeks it opened to the public. So is it a castle at all?

cards.headline: A castle from a stage set
cards.body: Ludwig wrote to Richard Wagner, whom he greatly admired, that he would build 'in the authentic style of the old German knights' castles'. The designs came from stage sets by the Munich scene painter Christian Jank, turned into plans by the architect Eduard Riedel. Neuschwanstein copies no real building. It mixes motifs from the Wartburg castle with castles from medieval book illustrations, a style called historicism.

cards.headline: Why a king built a dream
cards.body: In 1866 Bavaria lost a war to Prussia, and Ludwig was no longer a sovereign ruler. From 1867 he planned his own kingdom instead, in castles and palaces where he could be a real king. Romantic castles ran in the family: his father, Maximilian II, had rebuilt the nearby ruin of Hohenschwangau in a 'Gothic style' from 1832.

mascot.line: A knight would have been very confused by the plumbing.

cards.fact: Medieval on the outside, modern inside.
cards.context: The walls are brick, with pale limestone only as a skin. The Throne Hall is an encased steel construction: Level 8's metal, hidden inside a 'Romanesque' hall. Inside there was hot-air central heating, running water on every floor, toilets that flushed automatically, electric bells to call servants and telephones on two floors.

title: What Makes a Home
objective: After this level you can explain how climate shapes the way people build houses.
summary: Vitruvius: houses must suit their climate, sheltered in the north, open in the hot south. Roofs slope to shed rain, flat where it's dry. Vernacular: how communities house themselves.

cards.headline: A house built for Egypt would be wrong in Spain. Vitruvius said so.
cards.body: Remember Level 1's Vitruvius, whose book on architecture is about 2,000 years old? He opens its sixth book with climate as the thing that decides the style of a house: one style for Egypt, another for Spain, another for Pontus, another for Rome. This chapter tours the world's homes to see how right he was.

mascot.line: Level 1's commodity, in practice: a house is only useful if it works in its own weather.

cards.headline: Shut in, or open up
cards.body: His rule was simple. In the cold north, houses should be roofed over and sheltered as much as possible, turned toward the warm side. In hot southern countries, they should be built more in the open and face north. You do the same with curtains and windows. Vitruvius wanted the building itself to do it, to "amend by art what nature, if left to herself, would mar."

cards.headline: Read the roof
cards.body: Roofs tell the same story. The earliest ones were probably thatched with straw, leaves, branches or reeds, and they were usually set at a slope, or pitch, so rain could drain off. But flat roofs have long been common in the Middle East and the American Southwest, anywhere the climate is arid and draining water matters less. A flat roof is a bet that it won't rain much. In dry places, it's a safe bet.

cards.fact: ICOMOS has a name for homes like these: vernacular building.
cards.context: ICOMOS, the international council on monuments and sites, defines it as "the traditional and natural way by which communities house themselves." Its 1999 charter says you can spot it by a way of building shared across a community, a local character that answers the environment, and know-how passed on informally, from builder to builder. Level 1's architect hands over drawings. Here the plan lives in the tradition.

title: Igloos
objective: After this level you can explain how snow houses stay warm.
summary: Iglu means house in Inuktitut. Snow blocks climb an inward-leaning spiral into a dome. Compressed snow insulates, tiered floors hold the warmest air, and a lamp does the rest.

cards.headline: An experienced builder can raise a house of snow in one to two hours.
cards.body: In Inuktitut, iglu simply means "house". The snow iglu, the igloo, was a winter home and hunting-ground shelter of Inuit in Canada and Greenland. So how do you build a warm house out of something frozen?

mascot.line: Level 5's dome, rebuilt from snow in an afternoon. Engineers call that a good day.

cards.headline: A spiral of snow
cards.body: Builders pick hard, compact snow and cut large blocks with a knife of whalebone or metal. The top of the first ring is shaved into a slope: the first rung of a spiral. More blocks climb that spiral, each leaning inward, until they close into a dome, with the builder working from inside. Remember Level 5? A dome can rise ring by ring with no frame. An igloo is that trick, in snow.

cards.headline: Why snow, not ice
cards.body: Hard-packed snow is a good insulator, so the walls hold in body heat and the heat of an oil lamp called a qulliq. Solid ice would do worse: it holds heat less well than compressed snow. Some igloos have tiered floors, so people sleep up high, where it's warmer. Even melting helps: warm inside, bitter cold outside, and any thawing patch freezes again, making the walls stronger.

cards.fact: Inside an igloo, it's often just above freezing.
cards.context: That sounds chilly, and it is. Inuit traditionally kept their fur-lined clothes on indoors during the day. But with several people inside and a lamp burning, an igloo can reach about 15°C. The lamp was the heart of the home, where people cooked, ate, warmed up and talked. Not toasty, but home.

title: Yurts and Tents
objective: After this level you can explain the portable homes of nomads.
summary: The Mongol ger is a felt-covered wooden home that families take down, move and rebuild. Its roof poles meet in a compression ring; a tension band holds their outward push.

cards.headline: Some families can pack up their whole house and move it.
cards.body: In Mongolia, the traditional home is the ger, the round home that the West calls a yurt. It's light enough for nomads to carry, flexible enough to fold and pack, and sturdy enough to take apart and put back together. Wherever the herds find good pasture, the house follows, on horseback or a small wagon.

cards.headline: Wood, felt and rope
cards.body: A ger is a round structure: a wall, roof poles and a peaked roof on a painted wooden frame. Over it go covers of white felt and canvas, tightened with ropes of animal hair. Felt suits the cold, dry steppe, and families add extra layers when the temperature drops. The whole thing can stand up to Mongolia's fierce spring winds. And the name? Ger simply means "dwelling".

mascot.line: A band around the top holding everything in? Level 5's Florence dome would recognize that move.

cards.headline: A ring that squeezes, a band that pulls
cards.body: The roof is quiet engineering. Its poles meet in a center ring that holds them in compression. Where they meet the wall, they push outward: Level 4's thrust again. A band of rope, woven cloth or wire cable around the top of the wall holds them in tension. Squeeze in the middle, pull around the edge, and a yurt roof can span its room without inside posts, trusses or beams.

cards.fact: Taking down and putting up a ger is always a family job.
cards.context: Children learn by watching their elders. Men traditionally carve the wood, while women and men paint, sew, stitch and make felt, and cutting wool and making felt are usually done together. In 2013, UNESCO added the craftsmanship of the Mongol ger to its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. The house moves; the know-how stays in the family.

title: Mud and Adobe
objective: After this level you can explain why thick earth walls suit hot places.
summary: Taos Pueblo's adobe is earth, water and straw, never fired. Thick earth walls store heat, so rooms peak hours later. Water is adobe's enemy, so walls are replastered with mud.

cards.headline: Taos Pueblo's earth homes rose between about 1000 and 1450 CE.
cards.body: They're the multi-storied adobe homes of the people of Taos Pueblo in northern New Mexico, whose native language is Tiwa. Each home is owned by a family, which keeps it up in the traditional way, and the Pueblo has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1992. Mud isn't a lesser material. In the right climate, it's the smart one.

cards.headline: Earth, water, straw
cards.body: Adobe is earth mixed with water and straw, either poured into forms or shaped into sun-dried bricks. Level 1's timeline started here: sun-dried mud brick is one of the first building materials. The straw doesn't make the bricks stronger, but it helps them shrink evenly as they dry. At Taos, big timbers called vigas, hauled down from the mountain forests, hold up the roof of each story.

mascot.line: Same sun, same day. The wall just shows up to the heat a few hours late, on purpose.

cards.headline: A wall that stores heat
cards.body: Heavy walls have high thermal mass: they can store a lot of heat. When the midday sun beats on a thick earth wall, the heat soaks in slowly, so the room inside reaches its peak a few hours after the air outside. The effect is strongest where days and nights differ most in temperature. Here's an analogy: the wall works like a sponge for heat, soaking it up slowly and letting it go slowly.

cards.fact: Water is adobe's great enemy.
cards.context: Adobe is never fired in a kiln, so it never permanently hardens. It swells and shrinks with its water content, and the wetter it gets, the weaker it is. So adobe buildings last by shedding water and being cared for. At Taos, the outside walls are kept up by replastering them with thick layers of mud and straw. The plaster bonds so well because it's made of the same stuff as the wall.

title: Houses on Stilts
objective: After this level you can explain why some houses stand on stilts.
summary: Rumah panggung on the Musi River stand 1 to 2 m up so floods flow beneath. Alpine pile houses date from about 5000 to 500 BC. Every stilt is a post in compression.

cards.headline: Some of Europe's oldest villages stood on stilts.
cards.body: Around the Alps, from about 5000 to 500 BC, people built wooden houses on piles in or near water: on lakes, on river banks and in bogs. Why would anyone lift a house off the ground? A river community in Indonesia still gives the answer.

cards.headline: Let the flood pass underneath
cards.body: Along the Musi River in South Sumatra, communities build traditional stilt houses called rumah panggung. Raised about 1 to 2 m, they stay safe when floodwater reaches an adult's knees or waist, because the water flows under the floor instead of through the living room. The open space below also lets in air and light, cutting the damp that rots wooden houses. One move, two problems solved.

cards.headline: Standing on legs
cards.body: Stilts are Level 2's load path made visible. The whole house, and everyone in it, pushes down through the posts into the ground, so every stilt is in compression, like any post carrying weight. The Alpine builders planted theirs firmly: they burned each pile's end to a point, drove it deep into the mud, packed heavy stones around it and laid a platform of tree trunks and branches on top.

mascot.line: Over the water or over the mud? Either way, nobody's feet got wet at dinner.

cards.fact: Archaeologists still debate where the Alpine pile houses stood.
cards.context: In the mid-1800s, the Swiss archaeologist Ferdinand Keller argued they stood on platforms out over the lake water. Researchers now think they may have been built over swampy shore instead. Either way, the wet ground preserved their wood so well that 111 sites in six countries became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2011.

title: Roman Homes
objective: After this level you can describe Roman houses and apartment blocks.
summary: The rich Roman domus opened to the sky through its atrium. Everyone else lived in insulae: brick-and-concrete blocks of five or more stories, with less water higher up.

cards.headline: In the Roman Empire's great cities, a house of your own was for the rich.
cards.body: Crowding meant that by early imperial times, the private house had given way to the insula, a shared apartment block, for everyone but the very wealthy. So there were two ways to live in Rome: the rich family's domus, and everyone else's insula.

cards.headline: A house around a hole in the roof
cards.body: A wealthy Roman's house centered on the atrium, an open central court. Above it, an opening in the roof, the compluvium, let the rain in. Below it, a marble basin, the impluvium, caught the water. Larger houses added a colonnaded court farther in, the peristyle, with the family's private rooms clustered around it. Rain, delivered to the living room on purpose.

cards.headline: An island of apartments
cards.body: Insula is Latin for "island": a block rising from the street. Insulae were built of brick covered with concrete and were often five or more stories high, despite a height limit of about 21 m under the emperor Augustus. At street level were workshops and shops. Above them, homes reached by a shared staircase, taking light and air from the street and an inner court.

mascot.line: Top floor, great views, no water, fire risk. The listing would need creative writing.

cards.fact: In an insula, the higher you lived, the harder life got.
cards.context: Piped water reached only the lower apartments, so people upstairs had to use public facilities. Many insulae were cheaply built, and collapse and fire were constant dangers. Picture carrying every bucket of water up five flights, in a building that might burn. Nobody was bragging about the penthouse.
